'''Gabriel Stolzenberg''' (Brooklyn, New York, 1937 – Watertown, Massachusetts, 2019) was an American [[mathematician]] who taught at various academic institutions.

==Early years and education==
Stolzenberg was born in [[Brooklyn]], [[New York City|New York]] to Aba Stolzenberg (1905–1966),<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.example.org/ |title=Aba Stolzenberg |publisher=[[YIVO]] Archives |access-date=16 December 2023}}</ref> a [[Yiddish]] poet, and Florence Stolzenberg, also known as Bluma.<ref name=legacy>{{cite web |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/bostonglobe/name/gabriel-stolzenberg-obituary?id=2221734|title=Gabriel Stolzenberg|website=Legacy|access-date=16 December 2023}}</ref> His father and other Yiddish artists would often gather around poet Zishe Landau.<ref name=hyala>{{cite web |url=http://www.zchor.org/zisza.htm|title=Monograph: Zisha Landau z"l |last= Landau Bass|first=Hyala|publisher=Ada Holtzman|website=Zchor.org|access-date=16 December 2023}}</ref> His elder sister, Ethel, participated in a [[social club]] for young Jewish girls in [[Crown Heights, Brooklyn|Crown Heights]], called Faithful Friends Forever Club. This club was established around 1938. Ethel went on to receive a Ph.D. in [[Biophysics]] from [[Yale University]]. Later, she and her husband, Irwin Tessman, were inducted as members of the [[biological]] sciences [[Academic staff|faculty]] at [[Purdue University|Purdue]].<ref name=nypl>{{cite web |url=https://www.nypl.org/research/research-catalog/bib/b16500434|title=Faithful Friends Forever Club minute book|publisher=[[New York Public Library]]|access-date=16 December 2023}}</ref>

Stolzenberg attended [[Stuyvesant High School]]. At the age of sixteen, he went to [[Israel]], where he joined a [[kibbutz]] for one year.<ref name=obit>{{cite web |url=https://www.currentobituary.com/obit/238269|title=Gabriel Stolzenberg |date=19 November 2019 |website=CurrentObituary|access-date=17 December 2023}}</ref> Returning to the States, he entered [[Columbia University]] on a [[Ford Foundation]] [[scholarship]] to study [[Mathematics]]. He graduated in 1958 and went on to receive his [[Ph.D.]] in Mathematics from the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in 1961.

==Teaching==
Stolzenberg was [[Benjamin Peirce]] [[Tutoring|Instructor]] at [[Harvard]]. He also taught at [[Brown University|Brown]] and other [[Northeastern United States|northeastern]] institutions, such as [[Boston University]]. He held [[Visiting scholar|visiting positions]] at [[University of California, Berkeley|Berkeley]] and in [[Paris]]. His research field included the theory of [[Function (mathematics)|function]]s with several [[complex variable]]s and [[Banach algebras]]. He published primarily in the ''[[Annals of Mathematics]]'' and the ''[[Acta Mathematica]]''.<ref name=legacy/>

==Philosopher of science==
Stolzenberg, influenced by the work of [[Errett Bishop]],<ref name=photo/> was a [[Constructivism (philosophy of mathematics)|constructivist in the philosophy of mathematics]], as well as in [[Constructivism in science education|science education]].<ref name=const>{{cite journal |last1=Stolzenberg|first1=Gabriel|date=June 1978 |title=Letter to the Editor |journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]]|volume=25|issue=4|page=242 |issn=0002-9920|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/197806/197806FullIssue.pdf|access-date=16 December 2023|quote=Why should it be presumed that if I, a constructivist, were to review such a book I would have little choice but to object?}}</ref><ref name=photo>{{cite book |last= Halmos|first=Paul R.|author-link= Paul R. Halmos|date=1987|title=I Have a Photographic Memory|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ch2rmyplpUgC&dq=Gabriel+Stolzenberg&pg=PA515|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|access-date=18 December 2023|page=515|isbn=978-0-8218-1939-5}}</ref>

He was an active participant in the so-called "[[science wars]]",<ref group=n>Stolzenberg has contributed to the [[Talk:Science wars|talk page of the Science Wars article in Wikipedia]].</ref><ref name=replies>{{cite journal |last1=Stolzenberg |first1=Gabriel|date=February 2004|title=Replies to the Replies|journal=[[Social Studies of Science]]|url=http://math.bu.edu/people/nk/rr/rtrch.html|publisher=[[SAGE Publications]]|volume=34|issue=1|pages=115–132 |doi=10.1177/0306312704041343|access-date=18 December 2023|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=kinder>{{cite journal |last1=Stolzenberg |first1=Gabriel|date=February 2004|title=Kinder, Gentler Science Wars|journal=[[Social Studies of Science]]|url=http://math.bu.edu/people/nk/rr/rtrch.html|publisher=[[SAGE Publications]]|volume=34|issue=1|pages=77–89 |doi=10.1177/0306312704041336|quote=Review of Jay A. Labinger and Harry Collins (editors), ''The One Culture? A Conversation about Science'', University of Chicago Press, 2001|access-date=18 December 2023|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=faker>{{cite web |url=http://math.bu.edu/people/nk/rr/jd.html|title=The Invention of Jacques Derrida, Physics Faker|last1=Stolzenberg |first1=Gabriel |date=15 March 2004 |website=Boston University |access-date=18 December 2023}}</ref> defending [[post-modernism]] and constructivism against the positions held by scientists and philosophers, as well as against accusations of [[relativism]].<ref name=after>{{cite book |last1=Stolzenberg |first1=Gabriel |date=2000|editor-last1=Ashman |editor-first1=Keith  |editor-last2=Barringer  |editor-first2=Phillip | title=After the Science Wars: Science and the Study of Science|publisher=[[Routledge]]|url=http://math.bu.edu/people/nk/rr/bkln.pdf |chapter=Reading and Relativism: An introduction to the science wars|isbn=978-0-415-21209-0}}</ref> Solzenberg engaged publicly and for many years in a  dialogue with opponents of the postmodernist approach to sciences and of the use of concepts of physics, mathematics, or chemistry in philosophy and the social sciences,<ref name=reply>{{cite journal|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228614986|access-date=19 December 2023 |author-link1=Jean Bricmont|last1=Bricmont |first1=Jean|last2=Sokal|first2=Alan |author-link2=Alan Sokal|date=March 2004|title=Reply to Gabriel Stolzenberg|journal=[[Social Studies of Science]] |volume=34|issue=1|doi=10.1177/0306312704040491 |pages=107–113}}</ref><ref name=replytoreply>{{cite journal|url=http://math.bu.edu/people/nk/rr/rtrch.html|access-date=19 December 2023|last1=Stolzenberg|first1=Gabriel |date=March 2004|title=Replies to the Replies|journal=[[Social Studies of Science]] |volume=34|issue=1|doi=10.1177/0306312704041343|pages=115–132|issn=0306-3127|url-access=subscription}}</ref> attracting commentary across both positive and social sciences<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mB3y9IQKTmcC&dq=Gabriel+Stolzenberg&pg=PA121 |last1= S. Wiedenhof|first1=Jeroen |author-link1=Jeroen Wiedenhof |last2= Lubotsky |first2=Alexander|author-link2=Alexander Lubotsky |last3= Schaeken|first3=Jos |date=2009 |title=Evidence and Counter-evidence – Essays in Honour of Frederik Kortlandt: General Linguistics|page=416 |series=Studies in Slavic and General Linguistics|publisher=[[Brill Publishers]] |isbn= 978-90-420-2471-7| quote=Broad obstructive effects of language on progress in science have been intimated by Gabriel Solzenberg: despite a general awareness that language does seem to have the power to make us 'see things,' it is not taken seriously that language may be a determining influence and possibly a source of major error— for the contemporary scientist's own 'objective reality', the one into which he enters as a student and then shares with a community of fellow practitioners.}}</ref> and drawing wider attention to these issues.<ref name=ineffable>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=mB3y9IQKTmcC&dq=Gabriel+Stolzenberg&pg=PA121 |last= S. However, these and the relatively few other similar attempts I know of to take the role of humans in mathematics into account remain circumscribed by their adultocentrism/[[René Descartes#Philosophical work|Cartesian]] dualism.}}</ref>

==Private life==
Stolzenberg married Judith Levine (b. 1938)<ref>[https://radaris.com/~Judith-Levine/1412881138 Judith Levine]</ref> soon after graduating from Columbia in 1958.<ref name=obit/> He met his second wife, mathematician [[Nancy Kopell]] (b.1942), while they were both serving at the faculty of [[Boston University]].<ref name=dream>{{cite book |last=Wasserman |first=Elga Ruth |author-link=Elga Ruth Wasserman|date=2000|title=The Door in the Dream: Conversations With Eminent Women in Science|publisher=[[Joseph Henry Press]]}}</ref> Stolzenberg and Levine had two children, Nomi and Daniel Stolzenberg.<ref name=obit/>

Nomi joined the [[USC Gould School of Law]] faculty in 1988, with her research focusing mainly on the relationship of law with religion, [[liberalism]], [[psychoanalysis]], and literature.<ref name=USCG>{{cite web |url=https://gould.usc.edu/faculty/profile/nomi-stolzenberg/|title=Nomi Stolzenberg|publisher=[[USC Gould School of Law]]|website=Gould.USC.Edu|access-date=18 December 2023}}</ref> Daniel<ref name=letter>{{cite web |url=https://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2019-November/021777.html |title=Daniel Stolzenberg at Foundations of mathematics. Fwd: Gabriel Stolzenberg|publisher=[[New York University]]|website=CS.NYU.edu|access-date=18 December 2023}}</ref> went on to receive a PhD in [[History]] from [[Stanford]] and serve as a [[associate professor|historian]] of knowledge in [[UC Davis]], specializing in early modern Europe. In 2014, Daniel received the [[Howard R. Marraro Prize]] for the best book on [[Italian History]] published that year. He mainly researches the [[history of science]] and [[History of scholarship|scholarship]] from the [[Renaissance]] to the [[Age of Enlightenment|Enlightenment]].<ref name=early>{{cite web |url=https://history.ucdavis.edu/people/daniel-stolzenberg|title=Daniel Stolzenberg|publisher=[[University of California, Davis]]|website=UCDavis.Edu|date=14 June 2022 |access-date=18 December 2023}}</ref>

Gabriel Stolzenberg and [[novelist]] [[Cormac McCarthy]] were close friends.<ref name=corman>{{cite news |last=Pick  |first=Grant |date= December 1995 |title=The MacArthur Manner|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1995-12-03-9512030398-story.html |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |access-date=18 December 2023}}</ref>

==Death==
Stolzenberg died on 19 November 2019, at the age of 82, while being treated for a [[neurological disorder]] in [[Watertown, Massachusetts]].<ref name=legacy/>
